title: The Consonants
subtitle: C and G always hard; V as w; I as y; the clusters.
objectives: Pronounce C and G as hard stops in all positions.
Distinguish consonantal I (pronounced y) from vocalic I.
Distinguish consonantal U (pronounced w) from vocalic U.
Recognize and pronounce the clusters QU, X, and GN.

sections.heading: The hard rule for C and G
sections.body:
In Classical Latin, C and G are always hard. C is always k; G is always the g in 'go'. There is no soft c (as in 'city') and no soft g (as in 'gem'). This holds before every vowel, including e and i.

Cicero begins with a k-sound. So does cēna (dinner) and circus. The name Julius is pronounced YOO-lee-us, not JOO-lee-us. The first sound in genius is a hard g, not a j.

The softening of c and g before e and i happened later, during the medieval period. It is one of the clearest markers of the difference between Classical Latin and Church Latin. We teach the Classical pronunciation.

sections.heading: Consonantal I and U
sections.body:
The letters I and U each do double duty in Latin. Each can represent a vowel or a consonant.

Consonantal I is pronounced like English y (as in 'yes'):
  Iūlius — YOO-lee-us
  iam — yahm (now, already)
  māior — MY-yor (greater)

Consonantal U is pronounced like English w (as in 'wet'):
  vēnī — WAY-nee (I came)
  vīnum — WEE-noom (wine)
  vult — woolt (he wishes)

In modern printed editions, consonantal I is often written as J, and consonantal U as V. In this course we preserve the Roman practice: I for both, U for both. Context tells you which is which. When I or U appears before a vowel at the start of a syllable, it is consonantal. Otherwise it is vocalic.

sections.heading: The clusters: QU, X, GN
sections.body:
QU is always pronounced kw, as in English 'quick'. Q never appears without U.
  quī — kwee (who)
  quod — kwod (because, that)
  equus — EH-kwoos (horse)

X is a true cluster: k + s, as in English 'box'.
  rēx — reks (king)
  dūxit — DOOK-sit (he led)

GN is usually a true cluster (g + n), not the ny-sound of Italian 'gnocchi'. Some speakers nasalized it to ny in late Latin, but we preserve the earlier pronunciation.
  magnus — MAG-noos (great)
  signum — SIG-noom (sign, standard)

sections.heading: Listening drill
sections.instructions: Each consonant or cluster is spoken in isolation, then inside a real Latin word. Repeat after the recording.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Without looking back, answer each question.

items.prompt: How is the first sound in Cicero pronounced?
How is the first sound in genius pronounced?
items.answer: Like the g in 'go', not the g in 'gem'.

items.prompt: What does consonantal I sound like?
What does consonantal U sound like?
How do you know whether I or U is consonantal or vocalic?
items.answer: If it appears before a vowel at the start of a syllable, it is consonantal. Otherwise vocalic.

items.prompt: How is GN pronounced in Classical Latin?
items.answer: As two separate sounds: g + n, not the ny-sound of Italian.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 1.4 introduces stress and syllable quantity: how to tell where the accent falls in any Latin word.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can pronounce C, G, I, U, QU, X, and GN correctly in all positions without hesitation.
